title: Paper 1: The Language Task
description: The Question 3 language task (10 marks, 200–250 words): selecting powerful words, building the word–connotation–effect–purpose chain, and shaping a response examiners can credit.

notes.heading: The Task in Context
notes.body: The language task is the second half of Question 3, based on Text C, and it is worth 10 marks for a response of 200–250 words. It tests R1, R2 and R4 — understanding of explicit and implicit meaning and of how writers achieve effects and influence readers — and, strikingly, all ten marks are reading marks: there are no separate writing marks, though unclear expression still hides good analysis. For 2027–2029 the wording of the question was simplified and the length reduced to 200–250 words, and where the paper identifies particular words for you, they now appear in bold rather than underlined. Budget roughly 15 to 18 minutes. The short length is the point: this is a precision task, not an essay.

notes.heading: The Analysis Chain: Word to Purpose
notes.body: Every strong point runs through four links. WORD: quote the precise word or short phrase. CONNOTATION: what the word suggests beyond its dictionary meaning — its associations and emotional charge. EFFECT: what the reader sees, feels or understands as a result. PURPOSE: why the writer wants that effect here — how it serves the passage's aim. Worked example, from a storm description: 'the sea clawed at the hull'. Word: 'clawed'. Connotation: animal violence — scratching, tearing, something alive trying to get in. Effect: the boat feels like prey; the danger seems intentional, so the reader shares the crew's vulnerability. Purpose: the writer makes the crossing feel threatening so we experience the narrator's fear rather than just hearing about it. Stop one link early and the marks stop too: naming the word is selection, not analysis; stating the connotation alone is a dictionary entry; only the full chain reaches R4.

illustration.alt: A four-step chain diagram analysing the phrase 'the sea clawed at the hull': the word 'clawed' leads to its connotations of animal violence, then to the effect of making the boat feel like prey, and finally to the writer's purpose of making the crossing feel threatening.
illustration.caption: One phrase, four links: word, connotation, effect, purpose. A point is only creditable analysis when the chain is complete.

notes.heading: Selecting What to Analyse
notes.body: Choose three or four powerful words or short phrases — never ten weak ones. Powerful means loaded: heavy with connotation, imagery, sound or emotional charge. 'Clawed', 'shrank' and 'bled' each carry a paragraph of analysis; 'went', 'said' and 'nice' carry almost nothing, and grammatical filler like 'the' carries none. Keep selections short: a whole sentence cannot be analysed deeply in the space each selection earns, so quote two to six words. Spread your choices across the passage so your response shows the writer's range rather than one local habit. And if the question directs you to particular words or paragraphs, analyse those — the direction is part of the task, and ignoring it caps your marks. Selection is itself assessed: choosing the words that carry the passage's meaning shows R1 and R2 before your analysis even begins.

notes.heading: Killing the Empty Phrase
notes.body: Three sentences die in almost every script: 'this makes the reader want to read on', 'this grabs the reader's attention', and 'the writer uses language effectively'. Each claims an effect without specifying one, so each earns nothing. The test is specificity: what does the reader see, feel or understand at this exact word, in this exact passage? Replace 'creates a vivid image' with the actual image: 'the reader pictures frost furred over the window like mould, so the room feels neglected'. Apply the swap test — if your sentence about word X could be pasted under word Y unchanged, it is not analysis, because real analysis belongs to its word. The same discipline applies to technique labels: 'the writer uses a metaphor' only begins to score when you say what the comparison transfers and why the writer wants it transferred.

notes.heading: Patterns and Sentence-Level Effects
notes.body: Single words are not the whole task. Track image patterns: an extended metaphor sustained across a paragraph, or a semantic field — a cluster of words drawn from one area of meaning that quietly transfers its associations. A passage describing a city through 'arteries', 'pulse' and 'fever' is figuring the city as a sick body; naming the pattern and its effect is worth more than analysing any one of the three words alone. Sentence-level effects also belong here where they matter: a short sentence after a run of long ones lands like a blow; a list can overwhelm or accelerate. The technique vocabulary — metaphor, simile, sibilance, tricolon and the rest — is taught in the KS3 topic Figurative Language and the Year 9 topic Close Reading; revise those if the terms are shaky. In this task the label is only the doorway: marks live in the meaning, the effect and the purpose behind it.

notes.heading: Shaping the 200–250 Words
notes.body: The length is a design constraint, not a hardship. Open with one or two framing sentences naming the writer's overall aim and the dominant effect of the language — this gives the marker a map and stops your paragraphs drifting. Then write about three developed paragraphs, each built on one selection run through the full chain, or on one pattern you have tracked. Then stop. There is no conclusion paragraph: a summary of what you have just said spends a fifth of your budget buying nothing. Do the arithmetic: 200–250 words is roughly 60 to 80 words per analytical paragraph, so every sentence must carry a link in the chain. Well under 200 words reads as thin and under-evidenced; far over 250 suggests you have not selected, and it steals time owed to Question 4. Write the response you planned, at the length the task set.

notes.heading: How to Practise — and What to Avoid
notes.body: The quiz trains your selection and your judgement of stronger versus weaker analysis; the writing itself improves only through full attempts, so rehearse timed 200–250-word responses using this course's free-response practice sets with AI marking. In practice, hunt four failure modes. Paraphrase: restating what the quotation says in your own words — that is comprehension, and the chain's later links are missing. Technique listing: naming devices without meaning, the same failure as empty phrases with fancier vocabulary. Ignoring the steer: if the question identifies words or paragraphs, analyse those first. And mind-reading: claims about what the writer intended must be grounded in the words on the page — 'the writer wants the reader to feel the cold' is only creditable when you have shown which words create the cold. Ground every link, and the task becomes mechanical in the best sense: select, chain, move on.

flashcards.definition: The second half of Question 3: 200–250 words on how the writer of Text C uses language, worth 10 marks testing R1, R2 and R4 — all reading marks.
flashcards.example: Analysing three or four powerful choices from a paragraph and the effect of each.

flashcards.definition: Demonstrate understanding of how writers achieve effects and influence readers — the objective the language task exists to test.
flashcards.example: Explaining how 'clawed' makes the sea feel like a predator is R4; knowing the sea was rough is only R1.

flashcards.definition: Word → connotation → effect → purpose. All four links, every time; stopping early caps the marks.
flashcards.example: 'Shrank' (word) suggests diminishment (connotation), so the figure seems to dwindle before our eyes (effect), making the city feel overwhelming (purpose).

flashcards.definition: The associations a word carries beyond its dictionary meaning — the raw material of language analysis.
flashcards.example: 'Clawed' connotes animal violence and something trying to get in.

flashcards.definition: A word's literal dictionary meaning — the starting point of analysis, never the endpoint.
flashcards.example: 'Clawed' denotes scratched with claws; analysis begins when you ask what that suggests.

flashcards.definition: A cluster of words drawn from one area of meaning that transfers its associations across a passage.
flashcards.example: 'Arteries', 'pulse' and 'fever' in a city description figure the city as a sick body.

flashcards.definition: A comparison sustained and developed across several sentences or a whole paragraph rather than a single phrase.
flashcards.example: A sea described as clawing, hunting and finally devouring sustains one predator image.

flashcards.definition: A claim of effect with no content — 'makes the reader want to read on' — that could sit under any quotation unchanged.
flashcards.example: 'This grabs the reader's attention' earns nothing because it specifies no effect.

flashcards.definition: Choosing three or four loaded words or short phrases to analyse; the quality of the choice itself demonstrates understanding.
flashcards.example: Selecting 'clawed' rather than 'the' from the same sentence.

flashcards.definition: The one- or two-sentence opening that names the writer's overall aim and dominant effect before the analysis begins.
flashcards.example: 'The writer makes the crossing feel lethal, turning the sea into a predator stalking the boat.'

flashcards.definition: 200–250 words: a brief framing sentence plus about three developed paragraphs, and no conclusion paragraph.
flashcards.example: Roughly 60–80 words per analytical paragraph — every sentence must carry a link in the chain.

flashcards.definition: Restating what the quotation says in your own words — comprehension, not analysis; the connotation, effect and purpose links are all missing.
flashcards.example: 'The crowd roared — the writer shows the crowd was loud' only translates the quote.

questions.stem: How long should your response to the Question 3 language task be?
choices: No more than 120 words
250–300 words
200–250 words
350–450 words
questions.explanation: The language task asks for 200–250 words. The 120-word limit belongs to Question 2(a)'s summary, 250–300 words is Question 4's extended response, and 350–450 words is the Paper 2 composition — mixing up the limits costs either evidence or time.

questions.stem: From the sentence 'The fog swallowed the streetlamps one by one', which is the best selection for analysis?
choices: 'swallowed' — loaded with connotations of being consumed, and the verb carries the image
'streetlamps' — a concrete object the reader can picture
'one by one' — a short phrase that is easy to quote
'the fog swallowed the streetlamps one by one' — quoting the whole sentence covers everything
questions.explanation: 'Swallowed' carries the menace: it connotes eating, consumption and disappearance, so it supports a full analysis chain. 'Streetlamps' is a plain noun doing little work, 'one by one' is a functional sequence marker, and a whole-sentence quotation is too much to analyse deeply — strong selections are short and loaded.

questions.stem: Which response to the phrase 'Dawn broke like a bruise over the estate' is the strongest analysis?
choices: The simile makes the description vivid and grabs the reader's attention.
'Bruise' is a metaphor for the colour of the morning sky.
The writer compares dawn to a bruise, which is effective because bruises can be purple like some sunrises.

'Like a bruise' gives the dawn connotations of pain and damage — the new day arrives already hurt, so the reader expects harm to be normal here, and the comparison sets a threatening tone for everything that follows.
questions.explanation: The strongest answer completes the chain: connotation (pain, damage), effect (the day arrives hurt, harm feels normal) and purpose (setting a threatening tone). The first option is an empty phrase with no specified effect; the second mislabels a simile as a metaphor and stops at identification; the third stalls at surface resemblance — the visual match is the least interesting link and never reaches effect or purpose.

questions.stem: Which assessment objectives do the language task's 10 marks test?
choices: W1–W5 — it is fundamentally a writing task
R1, R2 and R4 — they are all reading marks
R3 and R5 only
R4 alone
questions.explanation: The syllabus assigns the language task 10 marks against R1, R2 and R4 — explicit meaning, implicit meaning, and how writers achieve effects. There are no writing marks attached, R3 (evaluate and develop ideas) and R5 (select for a purpose) belong to other questions, and R4 alone ignores the comprehension the task also demands.

questions.stem: What is wrong with the sentence: 'The writer uses emotive language to make the reader want to read on'?
choices: Nothing — it names a technique and an effect
It should say the language is 'excellent' to show evaluation
It claims an effect without specifying any — the same sentence could be pasted under any quotation unchanged
It is too short to earn marks
questions.explanation: The sentence fails the swap test: it specifies no particular effect, so it would fit any word in any text, which means it analyses nothing. Naming a technique plus a vague outcome is not analysis; calling the language 'excellent' swaps emptiness for empty praise; and shortness is not the defect — one specific sentence outscores a paragraph of filler.

questions.stem: A passage about a failing business describes its 'terminal quarter', 'haemorrhaging cash' and 'life-support loans'. What is the writer doing?
choices: Running a semantic field of terminal illness — the business is figured as a dying patient, so its decline feels irreversible
Using medical facts to inform the reader about the economy
Using three unconnected metaphors that happen to appear together
Exaggerating for comic effect
questions.explanation: The three phrases share one area of meaning — terminal illness — so they form a semantic field that transfers associations of death and inevitability onto the business. Nothing here is factual medical information; treating the phrases as unconnected misses the pattern, which is where the marks are; and the tone is ominous, not comic.

questions.stem: The first link of the analysis chain is…
choices: the effect on the reader
the writer's purpose
the connotation
the word or phrase itself, quoted precisely
questions.explanation: The chain starts with the word: a short, precise quotation anchors everything that follows. Connotation, effect and purpose are the later links — each depends on the one before, so beginning anywhere else leaves the analysis unanchored.

questions.stem: A response analyses eight different words within 230 words. What is its likely weakness?
choices: None — more words analysed means more marks
Each word gets under 30 words, so the selection was too wide and every chain is rushed and shallow
Eight quotations break the word limit by themselves
The response needed a conclusion to hold eight points together
questions.explanation: Eight selections in 230 words allows under 30 words each — too little to run word, connotation, effect and purpose, so every point stalls at the first links. Three or four fully developed selections outscore eight skimmed ones. The quotations themselves are short and legal, and a conclusion would shrink the analysis budget further rather than fix the depth problem.

questions.stem: A student writes: "'Shrank' suggests getting smaller." Which link of the chain is missing FIRST?
choices: The connotation-to-effect step — what the shrinking makes the reader picture or feel (for example, the figure diminished, intimidated), not just what the word means
The quotation — the word was never quoted
A technique label — the student should have called 'shrank' a verb
A line reference for the quotation
questions.explanation: The sentence reaches only a gloss of the word's meaning; the next missing link is what that suggests and does — the associations of shrinking and their effect on the reader. The word is already quoted, so the anchor exists. Technique labels and line references are not links in the chain at all: naming the word class adds no meaning, and examiners do not award marks for line numbers.

questions.stem: How should a language-task response open?
choices: By defining what language analysis means
With a sentence about the writer's life and background
With one or two framing sentences naming the writer's overall aim and the dominant effect of the language
By listing every technique present in the passage
questions.explanation: A brief framing sentence names the writer's aim and dominant effect, giving the marker a map for the paragraphs that follow. Defining the task wastes words on something the examiner knows; the writer's biography is irrelevant to the words on the page; and a technique list is feature-spotting before the analysis has even begun.

questions.stem: Which existing skills does the language task expect you to bring already learned?
choices: None — the task teaches you the techniques as you answer
Only spelling and punctuation
A memorised list of thirty device names
Technique vocabulary and close-reading habits (for example from the KS3 Figurative Language and Close Reading topics) — the exam applies them, it does not teach them
questions.explanation: The language task assumes you already know what metaphors, similes, sibilance and the rest are — the KS3 Figurative Language and Close Reading topics teach exactly that craft. The exam question only tests application. Spelling alone cannot carry an analysis, and a memorised device list without meaning is feature-spotting, the failure mode this task punishes hardest.

questions.stem: Which plan for a 240-word response is strongest?
choices: Ten short points with no development, plus a conclusion summing them up
A brief framing sentence on the writer's aim, three paragraphs each running one selection through the full chain, then stop
One long paragraph retelling the passage with quotations woven in
Two analytical paragraphs plus a long conclusion restating the introduction
questions.explanation: The strong plan matches the mark scheme's shape: a short frame, three selections each carried through word, connotation, effect and purpose, and no conclusion — at 240 words there is no budget for one. Ten undeveloped points never complete a chain; retelling with quotations is comprehension, not analysis; and a conclusion that restates the frame spends a fifth of the budget earning nothing.

questions.stem: The passage says the crowd 'roared'. A student writes: 'The crowd roared — the writer shows the crowd was loud.' What kind of response is this?
choices: Full analysis, because it quotes and comments
Evaluation, because it judges the writer
Paraphrase — it restates the meaning but never reaches connotation, effect or purpose
A summary error, because summaries must stay under 120 words
questions.explanation: The sentence translates 'roared' into 'loud' — that is paraphrase, which belongs to comprehension, and it stops before connotation (animal noise, a single beast), effect (the crowd feels unified and threatening) and purpose. It is not analysis despite containing a quotation, it is not evaluation because nothing is judged, and the 120-word summary limit belongs to Question 2(a), which is irrelevant here.

questions.stem: Where does the language task appear, and which text does it respond to?
choices: In Question 3, responding to Text C
In Question 1, responding to Text A
In Question 2, responding to Text B
In Paper 2, Section B
questions.explanation: The language task is the second half of Question 3, based on Text C, worth 10 of the question's 20 marks. Question 1 is comprehension on Text A, Question 2 is the summary task on Text B, and Paper 2 Section B is composition — none of them contains a language analysis.

questions.stem: Two responses to 'the house sighed in the heat'. Response 1: 'The personification makes the house seem alive yet weary, as if exhausted by the afternoon, so the reader feels the heaviness of the heat.' Response 2: 'This personification is very effective and makes the reader imagine the house clearly.' Why does Response 1 score higher?
choices: It is longer, and longer answers always score higher
It uses more technique labels than Response 2
Response 2 is actually stronger because it is more concise
Response 1 completes the chain — a specified effect (weariness, heaviness) tied to the device — while Response 2 claims effectiveness without specifying any effect
questions.explanation: Response 1 runs the full chain: the device, the connotation (alive yet weary), and a specified effect (the reader feels the heat's heaviness). Response 2 fails the swap test — 'very effective' and 'imagine clearly' could sit under any quotation. Length and label-count earn nothing by themselves, and concision without content is just a shorter empty answer.
